Rowan Ashcombe

From Openpedia, the free encyclopedia
American entrepreneur and fraudster (born 1992)
Not to be confused with another person of a similar name.
Rowan Ashcombe
BornMarch 5, 1992, Marlow, Oregon
OccupationEntrepreneur
Ashcombe in 2021

Rowan Elias Ashcombe (born March 5, 1992), commonly known as REA, is an American entrepreneur who founded the Quillex digital-asset exchange and was later convicted of fraud.[1][2] Quillex was once among the larger exchanges of its kind, and Ashcombe was a familiar guest at industry conferences.[3]

Ashcombe also founded Lantern Trading, a firm that bought and sold digital assets with its own money.[4] In November 2022 both businesses failed within the same week, after customers asked for their money back and Quillex could not pay it.[5][6] He was arrested in December 2022 and convicted in November 2023 on seven counts.[7]

Early life

[edit]

Rowan Elias Ashcombe was born on March 5, 1992, to upper-class Danish parents in Marlow, Oregon.[8][9][10] Both of his parents taught law at Calloway University, and the family lived a short walk from the campus.[11] He attended a private school in the next town and spent two summers at a mathematics camp.[12]

As a child he preferred board games and puzzles to team sports, according to a profile published in 2021.[13] A former teacher described him as quiet in class and quick with numbers, though often late with written work.[14]

The family spent most summers with relatives in Denmark, where Ashcombe learned to sail a small boat on a lake near their house.[15]

A neighbour recalled that he could talk about probability for an hour at a time and seemed puzzled when other people wanted to change the subject.[16]

Education

[edit]

Ashcombe studied physics at the Redmont Institute of Technology from 2010 to 2014 and added a minor in mathematics.[17] He lived in a shared house with eight other students and ran its weekly game night.[18] During his third year he took a summer job at a trading firm in New York, which offered him a full-time position after graduation.[19][20]

He later told an interviewer that he had considered an academic career but found laboratory work slow.[21] He left the trading firm in 2017 after a little more than three years there.[22]

Career

[edit]

In late 2017 Ashcombe started Lantern Trading with two former colleagues and a loan from an early backer.[23][24] The firm made its first large profits from differences between the price of the same asset in two countries.[25] By the end of 2018 it employed about thirty people and had moved its main office twice.[26]

Quillex opened in May 2019.[27] It offered contracts that let customers bet on future prices, and it charged lower fees than several older exchanges.[28][29] The company raised $900 million in July 2021 in a funding round that valued it at $18 billion.[30][31] It bought naming rights to a sports arena and ran television advertisements during a championship game.[32]

Ashcombe said repeatedly that customer money was kept apart from the money of his other businesses.[33] He told a legislative committee in 2022 that the exchange checked every account's risk several times a minute.[34]

The company moved its headquarters to a Caribbean island in 2021, citing clearer rules for exchanges.[35] Staff lived in apartments that the company rented near the office, and several of its executives shared one large house.[36][37]

In early November 2022 a trade publication reported that much of Lantern Trading's reported wealth consisted of a token that Quillex itself had issued.[38] Within days customers tried to withdraw about $5 billion.[39][40] Quillex stopped paying withdrawals on November 8 and filed for bankruptcy protection three days later.[41][42]

The administrator appointed to run the bankrupt company reported that its books were incomplete and that customer funds had been used to pay Lantern Trading's debts.[43][44] Several former executives pleaded guilty and agreed to testify.[45]

Two weeks before the collapse, the company had told customers in a public notice that their deposits were safe and available at any time.[46]

Employees later said they learned of the shortfall at a short meeting in the shared house, and many of them left the island within days.[47][48]

Regulators in several countries froze local accounts connected to the exchange while they tried to establish who was owed what.[49]

Customers formed groups online to share information about their claims, and some sold the claims to investment funds at a steep discount.[50]

Legal proceedings

[edit]

Ashcombe was charged in federal court with wire fraud, conspiracy and money laundering.[51][52] He pleaded not guilty and testified in his own defence for three days.[53] The jury deliberated for less than five hours before finding him guilty on all seven counts.[54][55]

In March 2024 a judge sentenced him to twenty-five years in prison and ordered him to forfeit about $11 billion.[56][57] His lawyers filed an appeal the following month.[58]

Both of his parents were sued by the new owners of Quillex, to return assets Rowan had given the couple in the form of cash and a home valued at over $32 million.[59][60] They disputed the claims and said they had not known where the money came from.[61]

Before the trial a judge revoked his bail after finding that he had twice tried to influence people expected to testify.[62][63]

The bankruptcy administrator said in 2024 that it expected to repay most customers the dollar value their accounts had held on the day of the filing.[64]

Inquiries in other countries

[edit]

Officials in Iceland opened their own inquiry later that winter and asked the administrator for the exchange's account records, which took 5 weeks to arrive and were incomplete when they did.[65]

Their interim findings, released the following summer, listed about 1800 affected customers in Iceland and recommended that exchanges keep client money with a separate custodian.[66]

Officials in Ghana opened their own inquiry later that winter and asked the administrator for the exchange's account records, which took 6 weeks to arrive and were incomplete when they did.[67]

Their interim findings, released the following summer, listed about 2700 affected customers in Ghana and recommended that exchanges keep client money with a separate custodian.[68]

Officials in Peru opened their own inquiry later that winter and asked the administrator for the exchange's account records, which took 7 weeks to arrive and were incomplete when they did.[69]

Their interim findings, released the following summer, listed about 3600 affected customers in Peru and recommended that exchanges keep client money with a separate custodian.[70]

Officials in Austria opened their own inquiry later that winter and asked the administrator for the exchange's account records, which took 8 weeks to arrive and were incomplete when they did.[71]

Officials in Uruguay opened their own inquiry later that winter and asked the administrator for the exchange's account records, which took 12 weeks to arrive and were incomplete when they did.[79]

Their interim findings, released the following summer, listed about 8100 affected customers in Uruguay and recommended that exchanges keep client money with a separate custodian.[80]

In Denmark, a regulator published a report 2 months after the filing that described how local accounts had been opened, who could move money between them and which records were missing when staff came to look.[81]

The same report counted about 5100 account holders in Denmark and said that most of them had learned of the freeze from a message shown when they tried to sign in on the morning after payments stopped.[82]

In Singapore, a group of former customers published a report 3 months after the filing that described how local accounts had been opened, who could move money between them and which records were missing when staff came to look.[83]

The same report counted about 6800 account holders in Singapore and said that most of them had learned of the freeze from a message shown when they tried to sign in on the morning after payments stopped.[84]

The same report counted about 8500 account holders in Japan and said that most of them had learned of the freeze from a message shown when they tried to sign in on the morning after payments stopped.[86]

The same report counted about 10200 account holders in Germany and said that most of them had learned of the freeze from a message shown when they tried to sign in on the morning after payments stopped.[88]

The same report counted about 11900 account holders in Australia and said that most of them had learned of the freeze from a message shown when they tried to sign in on the morning after payments stopped.[90]

Personal life

[edit]

Ashcombe described himself as a vegan and said he slept on a beanbag chair in the office during busy weeks.[105] He had pledged to give away most of his fortune, and a fund he financed made grants to research on pandemics before it closed in 2022.[106][107]
